chapters.name: Which sentence matters?
chapters.note: it matters... but how is it used?

cap.1: Rerunning the model told you which sentences in its reasoning really matter. It did not tell you how the model uses them. So you open the model up.
cap.2: Counterfactual importance (resampling) is black-box: it ranks sentences by how much they change the answer. The next question is mechanistic: what inside the model carries them forward?
cap.3: Bogdan, Macar, Nanda and Conmy (Thought Anchors, 2025) pair resampling with white-box attention analysis: if a sentence matters, some heads should attend heavily to it.

cap.1: A detective writes case notes line by line. Assistants run string from each new line back to earlier cards. Most spread it; a few always pick the same clue.
cap.2: Each head, at each later sentence, spreads a fixed attention budget over earlier sentences. Receiver heads send a big share to the same one or two sentences, from everywhere downstream.
cap.3: Sentence-level attention per head (token attention averaged within sentences). Receiver heads concentrate attention from all later sentences onto a few anchors, the ones resampling flagged.

cap.1: Read down a column to see how much string one card collects from every later line. For a receiver head, one column lights up all the way down.
cap.2: Rows are later sentences, columns earlier ones; each row sums to 1. You only get this grid with attn_implementation='eager': Flash attention never writes it out.
cap.3: Token attention averaged into sentence blocks, per head. vertical_score(s) aggregates attention to s from all later sentences; here the s2 column dominates every row.

chapters.name: Spiky, not wobbly
chapters.title: vertical scores: a wobbly head becomes a receiver head (toy)

cap.1: Two ways to be uneven. A wobbly head likes many cards a bit more than others. A receiver head loves one card. We want the second, so we measure spikiness.
cap.2: Rank heads by excess kurtosis, not variance. The wobbly head here has twice the variance, but the one-spike head has far higher kurtosis: a few very high scores.
cap.3: Excess (Fisher) kurtosis, the standardised fourth moment minus 3, is zero for a Gaussian and large when a few values dominate. Selectivity, not spread, is the target property.

cap.1: One assistant pins every string to the case-file cover. Very spiky, zero insight. Spikiness alone can fool you, so you also have to test what a head does.
cap.2: Attention sinks near the start soak up a constant share of attention: huge kurtosis, no reasoning content. Drop structural chunks (think markers) and depth-control the scores first.
cap.3: Sinks yield enormous, problem-stable kurtosis, and without depth control position alone creates spikes. After rank normalisation the baseline sits near 0.5 and real anchors stand above it.

chapters.name: Look, then touch

right.title: Touching (what settles it)
lines: suppress an anchor, then a dull sentence
the anchor must move the answer more

chapters.verdict: What you need: earn the head set twice, by suppression and by split-half reliability.

cap.1: Where assistants look is only a clue. The proof is cutting string: block the key card and the verdict should shift more than when you block a dull one.
cap.2: Current method: rank heads by kurtosis, keep about 16-20. Caveat: sinks and position can fake that ranking. What you need: split-half reliability plus a suppression contrast, scored by KL on the answer.
cap.3: Suppression recomputes attention (ARENA has you reimplement RoPE so the hook can) rather than masking returned weights. Suppressing a high-importance sentence should give the larger KL shift, and it does.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Black box and white box agree
A mechanism, not just a correlation
Capstone: a reasoning model the paper skipped

cap.1: Two different methods, rerunning the model and reading its insides, pointed at the same sentences. When methods agree like that, trust grows.
cap.2: Receiver heads turn 'this sentence matters' into 'this is how it gets used'. Reading reasoning like this is a step toward checking, and steering, what models think.
cap.3: Behavioural resampling and attention analysis converging is the strongest evidence interpretability gets. Bonus: reproduce the paper's Figures 4-6, or run it on a reasoning model it never touched.

coda.title: Make a head spiky: is it a receiver or a sink?

readouts.label: excess kurtosis (spikiness)
readouts.f: (() => { const v = range(10).map(i => 0.1 + 0.03*((i*7)%5)/4 + (i == anchor ? stare : 0) + (i == 0 ? sink : 0)); const m = mean(v); const d = v.map(x => x - m); const s2 = mean(d.map(x => x*x)); return (mean(d.map(x => x*x*x*x)) / (s2*s2) - 3).toFixed(2); })()

readouts.label: variance
readouts.f: (() => { const v = range(10).map(i => 0.1 + 0.03*((i*7)%5)/4 + (i == anchor ? stare : 0) + (i == 0 ? sink : 0)); const m = mean(v); return mean(v.map(x => (x - m)*(x - m))).toFixed(4); })()

readouts.label: what the suppression test would say
readouts.f: stare >= 0.2 && sink < 0.2 ? 'receiver: cutting s' + anchor + ' should move the answer' : (sink >= 0.2 && stare < 0.2 ? 'sink: just as spiky, cutting content changes nothing' : (stare >= 0.2 ? 'two spikes: kurtosis drops, the ranking gets muddled' : 'ordinary head: attention spread thin'))

caption.1: Push 'stare' up and watch spikiness climb. Then set stare to 0 and push 'dump on the start marker' instead: just as spiky, but meaningless.
caption.2: Kurtosis rewards a few big values, not general spread, and it cannot tell a sink from an anchor. That is why the head set must also pass the suppression test.
caption.3: Excess kurtosis is scale-free: one spike among ten scores gives roughly the same value whatever it sits on. Drop structural chunks, depth-control, then require the suppression contrast.

where_else: Citation networks: a few seminal papers collect citations from everything written after them
Induction and name-mover heads: the same attention-pattern toolkit, on tokens instead of sentences
Attention sinks: the same spike statistics flag a very different, content-free habit
Thought anchors by resampling: the black-box twin of this white-box method

hamming.what: An attention head that, from every later position in a reasoning trace, looks back hard at the same one or two key sentences.
hamming.when: When resampling has told you which reasoning sentences matter and you want the mechanism that carries them to the answer.
hamming.why: Finding those heads and showing that blocking them moves the answer turns a correlation into a mechanism, confirmed by two independent methods.

object.title: The string board
object.subtitle: One head's sentence-to-sentence attention in 3D: a receiver head lights one column all the way down.
object.f: c <= r + 1 ? (1 + 10*focus*(c == anchor) + 10*sink*(c == 0)) / (min(r + 2, cols) + 10*focus*(anchor <= min(r + 1, cols - 1)) + 10*sink) : 0

cap.1: An ordinary head. Each later sentence spreads its string over earlier cards, and no column stands out.
cap.2: Rows are reading sentences, columns earlier ones; each row sums to 1. Uniform attention means no anchors.
cap.3: Uniform rows give 1/n per cell, yet raw column means still vary with position: the confound depth control removes.

cap.1: A receiver head. From every later sentence, a big share of string goes to one card, so one column lights up all the way down.
cap.2: Every row downstream of the anchor puts heavy attention on it. That column's mean is the anchor's vertical score.
cap.3: One dominant column over a thin floor: across the column scores, that is large excess kurtosis.

cap.1: Move the anchor. The lit column follows, but only lines written after it can look back: nobody reads the future.
cap.2: Causal masking: only later sentences can attend to a sentence, so the lit column starts partway down.
cap.3: The attenders of sentence s are exactly the positions after s, which is why position confounds raw vertical scores.

cap.1: An attention sink: every row dumps its string on the start marker. Just as spiky, and it says nothing about reasoning.
cap.2: A sink head spikes on the first column in every problem. Kurtosis loves it; the suppression test exposes it.
cap.3: Sinks absorb a near-constant share of mass. Drop structural chunks and require the high-versus-low suppression contrast.

cap.1: The proof: block the lit column and the answer should shift more than when you block a dull one.
cap.2: Suppress attention to the anchor in these heads, then to a low-importance sentence, and compare the KL shift in the answer.
cap.3: Causal validation by KL between suppressed and unsuppressed answer distributions; a head set that fails the contrast is a sink detector.

predict.q: Your top heads all spike on the think marker, on every problem. Receiver heads?

options.t: Probably sinks: run the suppression contrast
Yes: being stable across problems is strong evidence

predict.why: Sinks give huge, stable kurtosis with no reasoning content. A real receiver head's anchor must move the answer more than a dull sentence when suppressed.

predict.q: Why rank heads by kurtosis rather than variance?

options.t: You want a few very high scores, not general spread
Variance is too slow to compute

predict.why: Kurtosis rewards selectivity. A head whose scores wobble widely can have high variance and still have no anchors.

predict.q: With Flash attention on, you cannot get attention weights. Why?

options.t: The fused kernel never materialises the matrix: reload with eager
Reasoning models do not use attention

predict.why: attn_implementation='eager' computes and returns the full attention weights; the fused kernel skips writing them out.

object.where: Anything ranked by 'a few huge values': citation hubs, attention sinks, hot keys in a cache.
